newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Firm oil price may lift North Sea activity in 1997.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Firm oil price may lift North Sea activity in 1997.

text.p: Strong oil prices, now boosted by heightened tension in the Middle East, could accelerate development of marginal North Sea fields and spur greater exploration activity in 1997, industry sources say.

While oil majors like Royal Dutch/Shell and British Petroleum are unlikely to alter their upstream plans -- generally based on an oil price of $14 a barrel -- smaller players could be encouraged by this year's rally.

"Next year we could see activity picking up slightly...Things could move rather more quickly given the good performance of the preceding 12 months," said Stephen Scullion of Edinburgh consultants Wood Mackenzie.
World benchmark Brent crude oil from the North Sea has averaged nearly $19.00 a barrel so far this year or about $2.00 above 1995 levels.

Other factors such as new technology, which has helped slash British offshore oil field costs by 75 percent since 1985, and the need to replace dwindling output from mature fields would normally override short-term price considerations.
But industry sources said any sign of an extension of this year's rally could prompt some companies to bring forward development plans or to redrill acreage abandoned for years.
With the northern winter looming, heating oil stocks severely depleted and the prospect of Iraqi sales receding, analysts expect prices to stay strong well into 1997.

"In terms of project planning, it might be a case of waiting until spring next year to see if there has been any easing of the inventory situation," said the director of a U.K.-based exploration company.
"If the price is still there then people may be willing to put a bit more money on the table," he said.
Industry sources said some smaller companies which are prepared to invest in projects on the basis of $17 Brent may accelerate development of proven reserves in the knowledge of guaranteed returns.

North Sea fields like Ross, with reserves of 75 million barrels of oil and operated by Talisman Energy, and Janice with reserves of 30 million barrels and operated by Kerr McGee, could be prime candidates, the sources said.
"Things that were originally scheduled for 1998 could be brought forward to 1997," said WoodMac's Scullion.
Higher world oil prices could also encourage smaller companies to snap up ageing fields which the majors no longer think are profitable.

Earlier this summer, Britain's outgoing energy minister Tim Eggar said he wanted to introduce in 1997 a new licencing system, applying only to mature fields, which would encourage "rapid and innovative exploration".
But a lack of suitable drilling rigs could hamper any attempt to accelerate developments or engage in new exploration drilling next year, industry sources said.
"There is a really tight rig market out there with increasing demand for development drilling after the number of government approvals in the last couple of years," said one.
With world oil production running at record levels, rigs are in demand in most offshore oil producing regions.
"It is still tight and there have been companies which have been forced to postpone or delay wells because of this problem," said Rebecca Gregory of Arthur Andersen Petroleum Services.
The shortage has forced some rigs out of cold storage, the latest leaving the Fal estuary in Cornwall for the United States only last month, she added.
Industry sources said semi-submersible rigs were currently commanding rates of as much as $150,000 per day, compared with $70-80,000 at the same time last year. -- London Newsroom +44 171 542 7930
